steps.label: 3 classical bits: 2³ = 8 possible strings
steps.sub: But only one is ever realized at a time — 3 bits of memory fully describes it

steps.label: 8 complex amplitudes, one per 3-bit string
steps.sub: Far more information than 3 bits is needed just to write them down

code:
2^3 = 8

amplitude per state = 1/sqrt(8) = 0.35355
probability per state = (1/sqrt(8))^2 = 0.125

sum over 8 states = 8 x 0.125 = 1.0  (OK)
caption: Measuring gives one of the 8 strings, each with equal 1/8 probability — like flipping 3 fair coins.

steps.label: To represent n qubits: 2ⁿ amplitudes
steps.sub: 10 qubits need 1,024; 50 qubits need over a quadrillion

steps.label: To read out: exactly n classical bits
steps.sub: One measurement, regardless of how large n grows

steps.label: This gap is why quantum computers can be powerful

steps.label: ...and why they're hard to simulate classically
